notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • The Indian monsoon is a large-scale seasonal wind system associated with seasonal changes in atmospheric pressure and circulation.
  • Its most visible feature is the reversal of prevailing winds between summer and winter.
  • The southwest monsoon supplies most of India's annual rainfall.
  • The northeast monsoon is especially important to southeastern India, particularly Tamil Nadu.
  • The monsoon is not produced by a single cause; it is a coupled land-ocean-atmosphere phenomenon.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Summer → Southwest Monsoon

Retreating/Winter Transition → Northeast Monsoon

2. Meaning of Monsoon
  • The term monsoon is derived from the Arabic word mausim.
  • Mausim means season.
  • The term originally referred to the seasonal reversal of winds over the Indian Ocean region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monsoon → Mausim → Season

3. Classical Explanation of Monsoon

The traditional explanation emphasises:

  • Differential heating of land and sea.
  • Summer low pressure over the Indian subcontinent.
  • Relatively higher pressure over the surrounding ocean.
  • Movement of moist oceanic air toward the land.

This explanation is important but incomplete by itself.

4. Differential Heating of Land and Sea
  • Land heats faster than water.
  • During northern summer, India becomes intensely heated.
  • The Indian Ocean warms more slowly.
  • A pressure gradient develops between land and ocean.
  • Moist air moves toward the low-pressure landmass.
5. Summer Low Pressure
  • During May and June, intense heating creates low pressure over northwestern India and adjoining regions.
  • This low-pressure zone helps draw moisture-bearing winds from the Indian Ocean.
6. Winter High Pressure
  • During winter, the Asian landmass cools rapidly.
  • Higher pressure develops over the continent.
  • Surface winds generally blow outward from land toward surrounding seas.
  • Therefore, winter is dry over much of India.
7. Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone
  • ITCZ is the zone where trade winds from the Northern and Southern Hemispheres converge.
  • It is characterised by low pressure and rising air.
  • It migrates seasonally north and south.
📌 Must-Memorise

ITCZ → Convergence + Low Pressure + Rising Air

8. Northward Shift of ITCZ
  • During northern summer, the zone of maximum heating moves northward.
  • The ITCZ shifts toward the Indian subcontinent.
  • Over northern India it is closely associated with the monsoon trough.
9. Monsoon Trough
  • The monsoon trough is an elongated low-pressure zone extending across northern India during the southwest monsoon.
  • It commonly stretches from the heat-low region of northwest India toward the Bay of Bengal.
  • Its position strongly controls rainfall distribution.
10. North-South Movement of Monsoon Trough
  • The monsoon trough does not remain fixed.
  • It shifts northward and southward.
  • These shifts produce alternating wet and dry spells.
  • A southward position often favours rainfall over central India.
  • A northward shift toward Himalayan foothills can produce reduced rainfall over much of central India.
11. Break Monsoon
  • A break in the monsoon is a temporary reduction in rainfall over large parts of the main monsoon region.
  • The monsoon does not completely disappear.
  • Rainfall may become concentrated along the Himalayan foothills and northeastern India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Break Monsoon → Temporary Weak Rainfall Phase

12. Active Monsoon
  • Active monsoon conditions produce widespread or above-normal rainfall over major monsoon regions.
  • Monsoon depressions and favourable trough positions often contribute.
13. Southeast Trade Winds
  • Southeast trade winds originate over the Southern Hemisphere.
  • They blow toward the equatorial low-pressure zone.
  • During northern summer, some of these winds cross the Equator toward South Asia.
14. Cross-Equatorial Flow
  • Winds crossing the Equator toward India are called cross-equatorial flow.
  • Earth's rotation causes their direction to change after crossing the Equator.
  • They become southwesterly in the Northern Hemisphere.
📌 Must-Memorise

SE Trades + Cross Equator → Southwest Monsoon

15. Coriolis Force
  • Coriolis force is an apparent deflection caused by Earth's rotation.
  • Moving air is deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • It is deflected to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Northern Hemisphere → Right

Southern Hemisphere → Left

16. Mascarene High
  • During northern summer, a strong subtropical high-pressure area develops over the southern Indian Ocean.
  • It is associated with the region near the Mascarene Islands.
  • It helps drive strong cross-equatorial winds toward South Asia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mascarene High → Southern Indian Ocean → SW Monsoon Support

17. Heat Low
  • A strong thermal low develops over northwestern India and adjoining Pakistan during summer.
  • It is called the heat low.
  • Its intensity affects the pressure gradient drawing winds toward India.
18. Tibetan Plateau
  • The Tibetan Plateau is a vast elevated landmass.
  • It becomes strongly heated in summer.
  • Its elevated heating alters upper-air pressure and circulation.
  • It is an important component of the Asian summer monsoon system.
19. Tibetan Plateau in Winter
  • During winter, the Tibetan Plateau becomes extremely cold.
  • It helps strengthen continental high-pressure conditions over Asia.
  • The seasonal thermal reversal supports monsoon circulation changes.
20. Jet Streams and Monsoon

Two major upper-air jets are important:

  • Subtropical Westerly Jet.
  • Tropical Easterly Jet.

Their seasonal changes are linked to monsoon onset and withdrawal.

21. Subtropical Westerly Jet
  • During winter, the Subtropical Westerly Jet lies south of the Himalayas.
  • It influences winter weather over northern India.
  • Before the southwest monsoon establishes, this jet shifts north of the Himalayas/Tibetan Plateau region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Winter India → Subtropical Westerly Jet

22. Tropical Easterly Jet
  • During summer, the Tropical Easterly Jet develops over tropical Asia.
  • It flows broadly from east to west in the upper atmosphere.
  • It is associated with the established southwest monsoon.
📌 Must-Memorise

Summer Monsoon → Tropical Easterly Jet

23. Monsoon Onset
  • Monsoon onset refers to establishment of persistent southwest monsoon circulation and rainfall.
  • It is not simply the first pre-monsoon shower.
  • The onset is characterised by increased rainfall, cloudiness, humidity and stronger winds.
24. Onset over Kerala
  • Kerala is the first major mainland region reached by the southwest monsoon.
  • Onset normally occurs around early June.
  • The exact date varies from year to year.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SW Monsoon Mainland Onset → Kerala

25. Burst of the Monsoon
  • The sudden increase in rainfall associated with monsoon onset is called the burst of the monsoon.
  • Temperatures often fall.
  • Humidity rises.
  • Cloud cover increases sharply.
26. Advance of the Monsoon
  • After Kerala onset, the monsoon advances northward.
  • It spreads rapidly along both western and northeastern India.
  • It subsequently covers central, northern and northwestern India.
27. Why Monsoon Advance Is Uneven

Monsoon advance depends on:

  • Pressure gradients.
  • Arabian Sea circulation.
  • Bay of Bengal systems.
  • Relief.
  • Upper-air winds.
  • Monsoon depressions.

Therefore, it does not progress as a perfectly uniform front.

28. Two Main Branches

The southwest monsoon is traditionally divided into:

  • Arabian Sea Branch.
  • Bay of Bengal Branch.
📌 Must-Memorise

SW Monsoon → Arabian Sea Branch + Bay of Bengal Branch

29. Arabian Sea Branch
  • The Arabian Sea branch carries large amounts of moisture.
  • It reaches India's western coast.
  • The Western Ghats force the winds to rise.
  • Heavy rainfall occurs on the windward side.
30. Western Ghats Effect
  • The Western Ghats run approximately parallel to the western coast.
  • Their steep western face forces moist monsoon air upward.
  • Kerala, coastal Karnataka, Goa and Konkan receive heavy rainfall.
31. Rain Shadow of Western Ghats
  • After crossing the Western Ghats, air descends over the Deccan Plateau.
  • Descending air becomes warmer and drier.
  • Rainfall decreases sharply on the leeward side.

Important rain-shadow areas occur in:

  • Interior Maharashtra.
  • Interior Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Parts of Tamil Nadu.
32. Arabian Sea Branch toward Gujarat
  • Part of the Arabian Sea branch moves northward along the western coast.
  • It brings rainfall to Gujarat.
  • Its effectiveness decreases farther inland toward western Rajasthan.
33. Arabian Sea Branch and Aravalli
  • The Aravalli Range runs roughly southwest-northeast.
  • Southwest monsoon winds often move almost parallel to it.
  • Therefore, the range does not force strong uplift.
  • Western Rajasthan receives little rainfall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aravalli Parallel Orientation → Low Rainfall in Western Rajasthan

34. Bay of Bengal Branch
  • The Bay of Bengal branch moves northeastward toward Bengal and northeastern India.
  • It carries abundant moisture.
  • Relief redirects it along several pathways.
35. Meghalaya Plateau Effect
  • Bay of Bengal winds strike the steep southern face of the Meghalaya Plateau.
  • They are forced upward.
  • Extremely heavy rainfall occurs around the Khasi Hills.
36. Mawsynram
  • Mawsynram lies in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya.
  • It is famous for exceptionally high average annual rainfall.
  • Orographic uplift is the major reason.
37. Cherrapunji / Sohra
  • Cherrapunji is also called Sohra.
  • It lies close to Mawsynram.
  • It also receives extremely high rainfall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mawsynram + Sohra → Khasi Hills → Heavy Rainfall

38. Bay Branch and Brahmaputra Valley
  • A portion of the Bay branch enters the Brahmaputra Valley.
  • Assam and adjoining northeastern regions receive heavy monsoon rainfall.
  • Surrounding hills enhance orographic rainfall.
39. Bay Branch along Ganga Plain
  • Another part of the Bay branch turns westward along the Ganga Plain.
  • It progressively loses moisture.
  • Rainfall decreases from east to west.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ganga Plain Rainfall → Decreases East to West

40. Monsoon Depressions
  • Monsoon depressions are low-pressure systems that frequently form over the Bay of Bengal.
  • They usually move westward or northwestward across India.
  • They distribute rainfall over central and northwestern regions.
41. Importance of Monsoon Depressions
  • Central Indian rainfall depends heavily on monsoon lows and depressions.
  • Their number, intensity and track influence seasonal rainfall totals.
  • Fewer or unfavourably tracked systems can produce rainfall deficiencies.
42. Low-Pressure Area vs Depression
  • Low-pressure areas are relatively weak systems.
  • Depressions have stronger organised winds and lower central pressure.
  • Both can generate widespread rainfall.
43. Monsoon Vortices
  • Monsoon rainfall is organised by several circulation systems.
  • These include:
  • Depressions.
  • Low-pressure areas.
  • Offshore troughs.
  • Cyclonic circulations.
44. Offshore Trough
  • A low-pressure trough often develops along India's west coast during the monsoon.
  • It enhances rainfall over Konkan, Goa, coastal Karnataka and Kerala.
45. Western Coast Heavy Rainfall

Heavy rainfall results from the combination of:

  • Moist Arabian Sea winds.
  • Western Ghats.
  • Offshore troughs.
  • Strong monsoon flow.
46. Monsoon Rainfall Characteristics

Indian monsoon rainfall is:

  • Seasonal.
  • Concentrated in a few months.
  • Unevenly distributed.
  • Variable.
  • Frequently heavy and episodic.
47. Concentration of Rainfall
  • Most regions receive a large share of their annual rainfall between June and September.
  • This concentration creates both water-resource opportunities and flood risks.
48. Rainfall Variability

Monsoon rainfall varies in:

  • Amount.
  • Onset.
  • Withdrawal.
  • Number of rainy days.
  • Intensity.
  • Spatial distribution.
49. Rainfall Reliability
  • Very wet regions tend to have relatively more reliable rainfall.
  • Arid and semi-arid areas show greater year-to-year variability.
  • Rajasthan is highly drought-prone partly because of rainfall variability.
50. Monsoon and Western Rajasthan

Reasons for low rainfall include:

  • Distance from Bay of Bengal.
  • Moisture loss during inland travel.
  • Weak orographic effect of Aravalli.
  • Continental location.
51. Monsoon and Ladakh
  • Ladakh receives little summer monsoon rainfall.
  • The Himalayas block moisture-bearing winds.
  • It lies in a strong rain-shadow region.
  • It therefore has a cold-desert climate.
52. Monsoon and Tamil Nadu
  • Tamil Nadu receives relatively limited rainfall from the southwest monsoon over much of its eastern and interior area.
  • Western Ghats create a rain-shadow effect.
  • Tamil Nadu instead depends heavily on the northeast monsoon.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → SW Monsoon Rain Shadow + NE Monsoon Importance

53. Southwest Monsoon in Tamil Nadu

Areas receiving more southwest monsoon rain include:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Western slopes.
  • Kanyakumari district.
  • Parts of Coimbatore-region highlands.

Interior and eastern districts generally receive less.

54. Nilgiris and Southwest Monsoon
  • Western-facing Nilgiri slopes intercept moisture-bearing winds.
  • Rainfall is considerably higher than in adjoining eastern rain-shadow areas.
55. Palghat Gap and Winds
  • Palghat Gap provides a low passage through the Western Ghats.
  • Moist winds can penetrate into parts of western Tamil Nadu through the gap.
  • It influences local rainfall and wind patterns.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Palghat Gap → Monsoon Wind Passage into Tamil Nadu

56. Monsoon Withdrawal
  • Withdrawal of the southwest monsoon begins when the continental low weakens.
  • Land begins to cool after the summer rainy season.
  • Winds and pressure patterns gradually reverse.
57. Where Withdrawal Begins
  • Withdrawal normally begins from northwestern India.
  • It then progresses southward and southeastward.
📌 Must-Memorise

SW Monsoon Withdrawal Starts → Northwestern India

58. Retreating Monsoon
  • October and November are traditionally called the retreating monsoon period over much of India.
  • The southwest monsoon withdraws.
  • Skies become clearer.
  • High humidity and warm temperatures can produce uncomfortable conditions.
59. October Heat
  • October heat refers to hot and humid conditions after monsoon withdrawal.
  • Days remain warm.
  • High humidity persists because the ground and atmosphere contain considerable moisture.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

October Heat → Retreating Monsoon

60. Northeast Monsoon
  • During the retreating season, winds over southern India increasingly blow from the northeast.
  • These are called northeast monsoon winds.
  • They are initially continental and relatively dry.
61. Bay of Bengal Moisture
  • Northeast winds cross the Bay of Bengal.
  • They pick up moisture from the warm sea.
  • They then bring rainfall to the southeastern coast of India.
62. Tamil Nadu and Northeast Monsoon
  • Tamil Nadu is the Indian state most strongly associated with northeast monsoon rainfall.
  • October-December is crucial for the state's water supply and agriculture.
  • Coastal and eastern districts receive particularly important rainfall.
📌 Must-Memorise

Northeast Monsoon → Tamil Nadu → October–December

63. Why Tamil Nadu Receives NE Monsoon Rain

Sequence:

  • Winds blow from northeast.
  • Cross Bay of Bengal.
  • Gain moisture.
  • Reach Coromandel Coast.
  • Rise/converge with weather systems.
  • Produce rainfall.
64. Coromandel Coast
  • The Coromandel Coast lies largely along Tamil Nadu.
  • It receives a major share of its rainfall during the retreating/northeast monsoon.
  • This is opposite to much of western India, which receives its heaviest rain in June-September.
65. Bay of Bengal Depressions in NE Monsoon
  • Depressions and cyclonic storms frequently form over the Bay of Bengal during October-December.
  • They enhance rainfall over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and adjoining southeastern India.
66. Tamil Nadu Cyclone-Rainfall Link
  • Cyclones can provide a large proportion of seasonal rainfall in a short period.
  • However, they can also cause:
  • Floods.
  • Storm surges.
  • Wind damage.
  • Crop loss.
67. Tamil Nadu Water Dependence

Northeast monsoon rainfall helps recharge:

  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Lakes.
  • Groundwater.
  • River basins.

It is crucial for both agriculture and urban water supply.

68. ENSO
  • ENSO stands for El Niño-Southern Oscillation.
  • It is a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon in the tropical Pacific.
  • It has three broad states:
  • El Niño.
  • Neutral.
  • La Niña.
69. El Niño
  • El Niño is abnormal warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • It alters tropical atmospheric circulation.
  • Many El Niño years are associated with weaker Indian southwest monsoon rainfall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

El Niño → Pacific Warming → Often Weaker Indian Monsoon

70. El Niño Is Not a Perfect Rule
  • Not every El Niño year produces drought in India.
  • Other factors may offset or reinforce its effect.
  • Therefore, El Niño should be treated as an important influence, not a guaranteed outcome.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

El Niño ≠ Automatic Indian Drought

71. La Niña
  • La Niña is abnormal cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • It is often associated with stronger-than-normal Indian monsoon conditions.
  • The relationship is also not absolute.
72. Southern Oscillation
  • Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric component of ENSO.
  • It involves fluctuations in pressure across the tropical Pacific.
73. Southern Oscillation Index
  • SOI is based on atmospheric pressure differences across the tropical Pacific.
  • It is one indicator of ENSO conditions.
74. Walker Circulation
  • Walker circulation is an east-west tropical atmospheric circulation associated with equatorial temperature differences.
  • ENSO changes alter the Walker circulation.
  • These changes can affect the Indian monsoon.
75. Indian Ocean Dipole
  • Indian Ocean Dipole, or IOD, refers to differences in sea-surface temperature between western and eastern equatorial Indian Ocean sectors.
  • It has positive, negative and neutral phases.
📌 Must-Memorise

IOD → Indian Ocean Sea-Surface Temperature Contrast

76. Positive IOD
  • Western equatorial Indian Ocean becomes relatively warmer.
  • Eastern waters near Indonesia become relatively cooler.
  • Positive IOD can sometimes support Indian southwest monsoon rainfall.
77. Negative IOD
  • Eastern equatorial Indian Ocean becomes relatively warmer.
  • Western sector becomes relatively cooler.
  • Negative IOD can sometimes suppress Indian monsoon conditions.
78. IOD and El Niño Together
  • IOD can modify the impact of ENSO.
  • A positive IOD may partially offset adverse monsoon effects in some El Niño years.
  • The relationship varies from year to year.
79. Madden-Julian Oscillation
  • The Madden-Julian Oscillation is a moving region of enhanced and suppressed tropical rainfall.
  • It travels mainly eastward through tropical oceans.
  • It can influence active and break phases of the Indian monsoon.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

MJO → Intra-Seasonal Tropical Rainfall Oscillation

80. Monsoon Intra-Seasonal Oscillation
  • Monsoon rainfall naturally fluctuates within the season.
  • Wet and dry spells occur on weekly to multi-week timescales.
  • These are important for agriculture even when seasonal total rainfall is normal.
81. Monsoon and Snow Cover
  • Snow conditions over Eurasia and the Himalayas can influence land heating and atmospheric circulation.
  • Historically, extensive Eurasian snow cover has been investigated as a factor affecting monsoon strength.
82. Walker Circulation and Monsoon
  • Strong tropical Pacific convection patterns can shift global circulation.
  • These changes influence rising and sinking air over the Indian Ocean region.
  • Thus Pacific Ocean conditions can affect rainfall thousands of kilometres away.
83. Monsoon Teleconnection
  • A teleconnection is a climatic relationship between distant regions.
  • ENSO's influence on the Indian monsoon is a major example.
84. Monsoon Variability and Agriculture

Monsoon variability affects:

  • Sowing time.
  • Crop selection.
  • Irrigation demand.
  • Crop yield.
  • Rural income.
  • Food prices.
85. Delayed Monsoon Onset

A delayed onset can:

  • Delay sowing.
  • Reduce early soil moisture.
  • Increase irrigation dependence.
  • Shorten crop-growing periods.

However, later rainfall can sometimes compensate.

86. Early Monsoon Onset
  • Early onset may support early sowing.
  • It does not guarantee a good monsoon season.
  • A later prolonged break can still reduce seasonal rainfall.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Onset Date ≠ Seasonal Rainfall Total

87. Uneven Distribution
  • Normal national rainfall can occur even when some regions face drought and others floods.
  • Therefore, spatial distribution is as important as national total rainfall.
88. Monsoon and Floods

Floods can result from:

  • Persistent heavy rainfall.
  • Monsoon depressions.
  • Himalayan runoff.
  • River-channel congestion.
  • Dam releases.
  • Urban drainage problems.
89. Monsoon and Drought

Drought can result from:

  • Delayed onset.
  • Long monsoon breaks.
  • Early withdrawal.
  • Weak monsoon depressions.
  • Poor spatial distribution of rain.
90. Meteorological Drought
  • Meteorological drought refers to rainfall substantially below normal.
  • It is distinct from agricultural and hydrological drought.
91. Agricultural Drought
  • Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture is insufficient to support crops.
  • Poor rainfall timing can cause agricultural drought even without extreme seasonal deficiency.
92. Hydrological Drought
  • Hydrological drought involves reduced water levels in:
  • Rivers.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Lakes.
  • Groundwater.
93. Monsoon and Groundwater
  • Monsoon rainfall is the main recharge source for groundwater in much of India.
  • Poor monsoon rainfall can reduce groundwater replenishment.
94. Monsoon and Reservoirs
  • Reservoir storage rises during rainy months.
  • Storage supports:
  • Irrigation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Hydropower.
  • Industrial use.
95. Monsoon and Hydropower
  • Strong monsoon inflows improve hydropower generation potential.
  • Weak rainfall reduces reservoir levels and hydroelectric output.
96. Monsoon and Indian Economy

Monsoon affects:

  • Agricultural output.
  • Food prices.
  • Rural consumption.
  • Electricity production.
  • Water availability.
  • Transport.
  • Inflation.
  • Disaster losses.
97. Monsoon and Kharif Crops

Kharif crops depend strongly on southwest monsoon rainfall.

Examples include:

  • Rice.
  • Cotton.
  • Maize.
  • Soybean.
  • Groundnut.
  • Bajra.
98. Monsoon and Rabi Crops
  • Rabi crops depend largely on stored soil moisture and irrigation.
  • Western disturbances provide useful winter rainfall in northwestern India.
99. Monsoon Rainfall and Rice
  • Rice requires considerable water.
  • High-rainfall and irrigated areas support extensive paddy cultivation.
  • Monsoon timing strongly affects transplanting and sowing.
100. Monsoon and Cotton
  • Cotton requires warm conditions.
  • Excessive rain can damage the crop.
  • Well-distributed moderate monsoon rainfall is favourable.
101. Monsoon and Millets
  • Millets such as bajra are better adapted to low and variable rainfall.
  • They are important in semi-arid regions.
102. Monsoon and Tank Irrigation in Tamil Nadu
  • Tamil Nadu has a long tradition of tank irrigation.
  • Northeast monsoon rainfall replenishes many tanks.
  • Tank systems are particularly important in districts without large perennial rivers.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

NE Monsoon → Tank Recharge

103. Monsoon and Kaveri Basin
  • Rainfall over the Kaveri basin comes from both southwest and northeast monsoon systems.
  • Upper catchments in Karnataka receive substantial southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Tamil Nadu's lower basin also depends significantly on northeast monsoon rain.
104. Monsoon and Western Ghats Catchments
  • Western Ghats receive heavy monsoon rain.
  • They form source regions for many peninsular rivers.
  • Rainfall there affects downstream reservoir storage.
105. Orographic Enhancement
  • Mountains can greatly amplify monsoon rainfall.
  • Western Ghats and Khasi Hills are classic examples.
  • Windward-facing slopes receive much more rain than leeward areas.
106. Foehn-Like Leeward Drying
  • As air descends on the leeward side, it warms and becomes relatively dry.
  • This intensifies rain-shadow conditions.
107. Monsoon Clouds
  • Deep convective clouds produce intense rainfall.
  • Cumulonimbus clouds are associated with heavy showers, thunderstorms and squalls.
108. Cumulonimbus
  • Cumulonimbus clouds have great vertical development.
  • They can produce:
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Lightning.
  • Thunder.
  • Hail.
  • Strong winds.
109. Monsoon Thunderstorms
  • Thunderstorms occur during both pre-monsoon and monsoon seasons.
  • They are more common when strong atmospheric instability is present.
110. Pre-Monsoon Heat and Monsoon
  • Intense pre-monsoon heating contributes to thermal low-pressure development.
  • However, the onset depends on large-scale atmospheric circulation, not temperature alone.
111. Western Disturbances and Monsoon Transition
  • Western disturbances dominate much of northern India's winter precipitation.
  • Their influence declines as summer circulation and monsoon conditions strengthen.
112. Monsoon and Himalayan Barrier
  • Himalayas prevent moisture-bearing monsoon air from moving directly into Central Asia.
  • Winds are redirected along the mountain barrier.
  • This promotes rainfall over northern India.
113. Monsoon and Brahmaputra Valley
  • The valley channels moist air eastward and northeastward.
  • Surrounding highlands enhance rainfall.
114. Monsoon and Ganga Plain
  • Bay of Bengal moisture moves westward.
  • Rainfall progressively declines toward western Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan.
115. Monsoon and Central India
  • Central India lies along common tracks of Bay of Bengal depressions.
  • Therefore, these systems are crucial for rainfall over Madhya Pradesh and adjoining states.
116. Monsoon and Western Coast
  • Western coast rainfall is more continuous during strong monsoon periods because of persistent moist flow against the Western Ghats.
117. Monsoon and Eastern Coast
  • Much of the eastern coast receives southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • However, southeastern Tamil Nadu receives its major seasonal maximum later during the northeast monsoon.
118. Monsoon and Islands
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands receive substantial rainfall from monsoon systems.
  • Their maritime location leads to high humidity and limited annual temperature variation.
  • Lakshadweep also experiences strong southwest monsoon influence.
119. Monsoon Withdrawal and Cyclones
  • As southwest monsoon withdraws, the Bay of Bengal remains warm.
  • Tropical depressions and cyclones become important.
  • Southeastern India can receive very heavy rainfall.
120. Northeast Monsoon vs Southwest Monsoon

Southwest Monsoon:

  • Mainly June-September.
  • Winds broadly southwest to northeast.
  • Major rain season for most of India.

Northeast Monsoon:

  • Mainly October-December over southeastern India.
  • Winds broadly northeast to southwest.
  • Major rain season for Tamil Nadu.
121. Southwest Monsoon vs Western Disturbances

Southwest monsoon:

  • Tropical oceanic circulation.
  • Summer rainfall.

Western disturbances:

  • Extratropical systems.
  • Winter rainfall in northwestern India.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Western Disturbance ≠ Monsoon Depression

122. Monsoon Depression vs Tropical Cyclone

Monsoon depression:

  • Usually weaker.
  • Often forms during summer monsoon.
  • Produces widespread rain.

Tropical cyclone:

  • Stronger organised storm.
  • Higher wind speeds.
  • More destructive coastal impacts.
123. Monsoon and Cyclonic Storms
  • Cyclonic storms can occur before and after the main southwest monsoon season.
  • Bay of Bengal storms are especially important for the east coast.
124. Monsoon and Climate Unity
  • India's diverse regions share a common seasonal monsoon rhythm.
  • This gives the country a degree of climatic unity despite strong regional variation.
125. Why Monsoon Is Called a Unifying Bond

The monsoon influences:

  • Agriculture.
  • Rivers.
  • Vegetation.
  • Festivals.
  • Food production.
  • Rural economy.
  • Water storage.

Therefore, seasonal rainfall affects much of Indian life simultaneously.

126. Monsoon Forecasting

Forecasting uses observations of:

  • Ocean temperatures.
  • Atmospheric pressure.
  • Winds.
  • Snow conditions.
  • ENSO.
  • IOD.
  • Satellite data.
  • Numerical weather models.
127. Satellite Role

Weather satellites monitor:

  • Clouds.
  • Water vapour.
  • Cyclones.
  • Sea-surface conditions.
  • Rain-bearing systems.
128. Radar Role

Weather radar helps track:

  • Rainfall intensity.
  • Thunderstorms.
  • Cyclones near land.
  • Movement of rain systems.
129. Rain Gauge Role
  • Rain gauges provide ground-based rainfall measurements.
  • Networks of stations are needed because rainfall varies greatly over short distances.
130. Monsoon and Climate Change
  • Warming can influence atmospheric moisture, extreme rainfall and monsoon variability.
  • Changes in average rainfall and rainfall intensity need not occur in the same direction.
  • Detailed climate-change facts belong to the later Climate Change chapter.
131. Tamil Nadu — High-Yield Monsoon Facts
  • Tamil Nadu receives rainfall from both southwest and northeast monsoons.
  • Northeast monsoon is especially important.
  • October-December is crucial.
  • Coromandel Coast receives retreating monsoon rainfall.
  • Bay of Bengal cyclones enhance seasonal rainfall.
  • Western Ghats create rain-shadow conditions over much of the state.
  • Nilgiris receive substantial southwest monsoon rainfall.
  • Palghat Gap allows some monsoon winds into western Tamil Nadu.
  • Tanks are strongly dependent on seasonal rain.

133. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Mausim → Season.
  • Summer → Heat low.
  • ITCZ → Monsoon trough.
  • SE trades → Cross-equatorial flow.
  • Mascarene High → Southern Indian Ocean.
  • Summer upper jet → Tropical Easterly Jet.
  • Winter upper jet → Subtropical Westerly Jet.
  • Onset → Kerala.
  • SW branches → Arabian + Bay.
  • Arabian branch → Western Ghats.
  • Bay branch → Meghalaya.
  • Mawsynram → Khasi Hills.

  • Withdrawal → Northwest India first.
  • October heat → Retreating monsoon.

  • La Niña → Pacific cooling.
  • IOD → Indian Ocean temperature contrast.
  • MJO → Intra-seasonal tropical variability.
134. TNPSC Traps
  • Monsoon is not caused only by land-sea heating.
  • ITCZ shifts seasonally.
  • Monsoon trough is associated with summer low pressure over northern India.
  • Southeast trade winds cross the Equator and become southwest winds.
  • Coriolis deflection is rightward in Northern Hemisphere.
  • Mascarene High lies in the southern Indian Ocean.
  • Tropical Easterly Jet is associated with summer monsoon.
  • Subtropical Westerly Jet is prominent south of Himalayas in winter.
  • The first shower is not automatically official monsoon onset.
  • Southwest monsoon has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches.
  • Western Ghats produce a major rain shadow.
  • Aravalli orientation contributes to low rainfall in western Rajasthan.
  • Mawsynram lies in Khasi Hills.
  • Rainfall decreases east-to-west along much of the Ganga Plain.
  • Break monsoon does not mean monsoon withdrawal.
  • Bay of Bengal depressions carry rain into central India.
  • Withdrawal starts from northwestern India.
  • Tamil Nadu receives major rainfall after the southwest monsoon begins retreating.
  • Northeast winds become moist only after crossing Bay of Bengal.
  • El Niño does not always produce drought.
  • La Niña does not guarantee excess rainfall.
  • IOD can strengthen or weaken ENSO influence.
  • Early onset does not guarantee good seasonal rainfall.
  • Seasonal total rainfall alone does not show regional drought conditions.
  • Tamil Nadu tanks depend heavily on seasonal monsoon recharge.
  • Western disturbances are not tropical monsoon systems.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Monsoon word derived from? → Arabic mausim.
  • Mausim means? → Season.
  • Core feature of monsoon? → Seasonal wind reversal.
  • Main rainy monsoon of India? → Southwest monsoon.
  • Main monsoon for Tamil Nadu? → Northeast monsoon.
  • Traditional basic cause of monsoon? → Differential heating of land and sea.
  • Summer pressure over northwestern India? → Low pressure.
  • Winter pressure over continental India? → Higher pressure.
  • ITCZ full form? → Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone.
  • Nature of ITCZ? → Low-pressure convergence zone.
  • Summer ITCZ over India called broadly? → Monsoon trough.
  • What does monsoon trough movement produce? → Wet and dry rainfall spells.
  • Break monsoon means? → Temporary reduction of monsoon rainfall.
  • Active monsoon means? → Widespread stronger rainfall phase.
  • Which Southern Hemisphere winds cross the Equator? → Southeast trade winds.
  • After crossing the Equator, they become? → Southwest monsoon winds.
  • Coriolis deflection in Northern Hemisphere? → Right.
  • High-pressure system helping monsoon flow from southern Indian Ocean? → Mascarene High.
  • Summer low over northwest India called? → Heat low.
  • Large elevated landmass important to summer monsoon heating? → Tibetan Plateau.
  • Winter jet over northern India? → Subtropical Westerly Jet.
  • Summer monsoon jet? → Tropical Easterly Jet.
  • First major mainland state reached by SW monsoon? → Kerala.
  • Sudden onset rainfall called? → Burst of monsoon.
  • Two branches of SW monsoon? → Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches.
  • Which branch gives heavy rain to western coast? → Arabian Sea branch.
  • Main mountain responsible? → Western Ghats.
  • Dry region east of mountain barrier called? → Rain shadow.
  • Why does western Rajasthan receive little rainfall? → Inland location, moisture loss and Aravalli orientation.
  • Which branch produces very heavy rainfall in Meghalaya? → Bay of Bengal branch.
  • Very wet location in Khasi Hills? → Mawsynram.
  • Cherrapunji's other name? → Sohra.
  • Monsoon rainfall across Ganga Plain decreases generally from? → East to west.
  • Major rain-bearing systems moving from Bay into central India? → Monsoon depressions.
  • What is an offshore trough? → Low-pressure trough along a coast that enhances rainfall.
  • Which coast is strongly affected by offshore trough during SW monsoon? → Western coast.
  • Where does SW monsoon withdrawal usually begin? → Northwestern India.
  • October heat occurs during? → Retreating monsoon.
  • Main NE monsoon months in Tamil Nadu? → October-December.
  • Why does NE monsoon bring rain to Tamil Nadu? → Winds cross Bay of Bengal and gain moisture.
  • Which Tamil Nadu coast gets major NE monsoon rain? → Coromandel Coast.
  • What strengthens Tamil Nadu NE monsoon rainfall? → Bay of Bengal depressions and cyclones.
  • Why does much of Tamil Nadu receive less SW monsoon rain? → Western Ghats rain-shadow effect.
  • Important gap allowing winds into western Tamil Nadu? → Palghat Gap.
  • ENSO full form? → El Niño-Southern Oscillation.
  • El Niño means? → Abnormal warming of central/eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • La Niña means? → Abnormal cooling of central/eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • El Niño's usual Indian association? → Often weaker southwest monsoon.
  • Does El Niño always cause drought? → No.
  • Does La Niña always cause excess rainfall? → No.
  • IOD full form? → Indian Ocean Dipole.
  • Positive IOD means? → Western equatorial Indian Ocean relatively warmer than eastern region near Indonesia.
  • MJO full form? → Madden-Julian Oscillation.
  • MJO affects? → Intra-seasonal active and break rainfall phases.
  • Does early monsoon onset guarantee good rainfall? → No.
  • Does normal all-India rainfall mean every region receives normal rain? → No.
  • Meteorological drought means? → Rainfall deficiency.
  • Agricultural drought means? → Inadequate soil moisture.
  • Hydrological drought means? → Reduced rivers, reservoirs and groundwater.
  • Main recharge season for much of India's groundwater? → Monsoon season.
  • Major monsoon-dependent cropping season? → Kharif.
  • Tamil Nadu traditional water-storage system heavily dependent on monsoon? → Tanks.
